newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU meat talks continue as deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU meat talks continue as deadline looms.

text.p: U.S. and European officials continued meeting into Tuesday evening in an attempt to settle a long-running trans-Atlantic dispute over meat import regulations before an April 1 deadline.

Negotiators were said to be stalled on a number of issues, and meat industry sources were not optimistic that the complicated areas of disagreement would be resolved in time to prevent threatened trade action by both sides next month.
At best, sources said the deadline may be extended.
"I don't think either side has the ability to wrap it up this week ... so it's a question of what will happen on April 1," said a meat industry official familiar with the talks.
The dispute threatens to disrupt several hundred millions of dollars of trade in meat, poultry, dairy and pet food products betweem the United States and the European Union.
The talks center on so-called veterinary equivalency rules under which each side would accept meat and meat products from the other even if their safety inspection methods differ.
The negotiators met Monday and Tuesday and were planning to hold talks Wednesday after the Tuesday evening session.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Tuesday morning that the United States was firm in its plans to curtail meat shipments from the European Union if there was no agreement.
"We are resolute. We have to respond with clarity," Glickman told Reuters following a breakfast speech. "I still hope we can work something out in the next week."

The EU has said it will implement new veterinary and sanitary controls beginning April 1. The Agriculture Department has said it would retaliate for any cutback in access to EU markets caused by the new rules.
The dispute has run for years, and the U.S. meat industry has urged the administration to take a hard line and either finally settle the issue or take retaliatory action.

"It's time to get serious and to get this resolved," said Alisa Harrison of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association. "We've asked the administration not to extend the deadline ... We've asked the administration to retaliate if no agreement is reached."
"Our meat insepction here in the United States is one of the tops in the world, and to imply that in some ways our system is inferior is preposterous," Harrison added.

If no agreement is reached, what the U.S. action would be is still uncertain. The administration could restrict all meat and meat product imports from Europe, which most industry officials agreed is unlikely, or apply stricter standards on European meat-packing plants on a case-by-case basis.
Europe could restrict imports of U.S. diary, poultry, pet food and other related items.
